speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: It is where we learn our first lessons about values that will shape our character and identity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: Families also provide a safe environment to nurture our children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: A strong family can also help children develop into resilient adults who will then go on to contribute to society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: While parenthood is a fruitful journey, it is also one that has its challenges.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: The 2021 Marriage and Parenthood Survey shows that the ability to manage costs of childraising as well as work and family commitments are key considerations of couples when making parenthood decisions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: The Government is committed to support couples as they embark on their parenting journey.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: One of the key ways in which we do so is through the Marriage and Parenthood Package, which comprises a suite of measures to support parents, such as parental leave and benefits and the Baby Bonus schemes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: To ensure that the Marriage and Parenthood Package continues to meet the evolving needs of parents, we periodically review our policies and introduce enhancements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: Since the Child Development Co-Savings Act was introduced more than 20 years ago, we have made amendments to effect enhancements, such as the introduction of Government-Paid Paternity Leave and Shared Parental Leave.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: We have also introduced the Government-Paid Maternity Benefits to support mothers who are ineligible for the Government-Paid Maternity Leave because they are on short-term contracts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: The latest round of enhancements in 2021 saw the introduction of the Government-Paid Paternity Benefit and Government-Paid Adoption Benefits to support working fathers and adoptive mothers who are shorter-term contract workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: The Child Development Co-Savings (Amendment) Bill that is currently before this House seeks to give effect to the leave enhancements announced at Budget 2023.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: This includes the enhancements to our paternity payment and reimbursement schemes, namely, the increase of Government-Paid Paternity Leave by two weeks on a voluntary basis and increase of the Government-Paid Paternity Benefit in parallel as well as the extension of the Unpaid Infant Care Leave.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: First, clauses 7, 8, 9 and 10 set out the main provisions for the enhancements to our paternity payment and reimbursement schemes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: These enhancements apply to fathers of children born on or after 1 January 2024 or with an estimated date of delivery on or after 1 January 2024 as well as adoptive fathers where the eligibility date of the application to adopt a child is on or after 1 January 2024.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: The additional two weeks of paternity leave will be implemented on a voluntary basis so that employers have more time to adjust.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: The reimbursement limits for employers will, as a result, be doubled to cover both the compulsory paternity leave and additional paternity leave.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: Employers who are ready to grant the extra paternity leave to eligible employees will be reimbursed by the Government from 1 January 2024.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: Clause 8 will double the Government-Paid Paternity Benefit from the current 14 days to 28 days of an eligible father’s total income.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: Fathers who cannot qualify for paternity leave under CDCA due to their employment arrangements may be eligible for this enhanced Government-Paid Paternity Benefit, which is a cash benefit in lieu of the paternity leave.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: Clauses 7 and 9 will also effectively double the limits for the Government’s payment to eligible self-employed fathers for their loss of income when they stop work to care for their children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: We are encouraged by the increase in take-up rates of Government-Paid Paternity Leave since its introduction 10 years ago.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: Today, more than half of our fathers take paternity leave.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: Nevertheless, we want to encourage more fathers to be more involved in their children’s growing years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: The enhancements we are making to the Government-Paid Paternity Leave and Government-Paid Paternity Benefit are critical steps that the Government is making towards normalising paternal involvement in our society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: We hope that this increase will allow fathers to be more involved in caring for their children from the very beginning.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: Research has shown that children whose fathers are more involved have better outcomes in their physical, cognitive and emotional development.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: Locally, data from the Singapore Longitudinal Early Development Study, or SG LEADS in short, has shown that paternity leave utilisation can increase marital satisfaction.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: It also found that taking a longer duration of paternity leave would significantly reduce children’s behaviour problems through the mediating effects of family dynamics.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: The Bill also contains other clauses to improve operational efficiency and clarity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: The Approved Persons are designated persons responsible for overseeing the administration of the Child Development Account (CDA), otherwise known as CDA funds, which can only be used at Approved Institutions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: They ensure that the CDA funds are withdrawn according to the prescribed usages in the Child Development Co-saving Regulations (CDCR).

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: This will ensure that the relevant benefits are disbursed according to the design of the schemes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: The Government is committed to this cause and will continue to review our measures to provide greater assurance to young couples as they think about starting and growing their families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: Beyond our support schemes, it is important that, as a society, we also strive towards building a family-friendly culture.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: One key challenge that couples contemplating parenthood often grapple with is how to balance their caregiving and professional commitments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: Hence, it is most heartening when we see employers step up to address this issue.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: Take the example of Telstra, a global telecommunications and technology company that has been operating in Singapore for more than 20 years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: They have moved to review their paternity leave policy immediately after the announcement and started offering the additional two weeks of paternity leave to their employees from 1 July 2023 before Government reimbursement will commence from 1 January 2024.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: Since then, some fathers have enjoyed the additional paternity leave and feedback has been positive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: On top of offering additional paternity leave, Telstra has also adopted other family-friendly work practices, such as a flexible working policy where employees can choose their work hours and location, with no mandated number of days in the office.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: This is a commendable demonstration of commitment towards adopting family-friendly practices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: By doing so, employers will also benefit as they can improve their talent attraction and retention outcomes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: Over time, we hope to see many more companies making it a priority to create a family-friendly workplace culture.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: The Bill before this House today is part of our greater efforts to create a Singapore that values and supports family well-being.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: The Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) is committed to supporting Singaporeans as they embark on their parenthood journey and will continue to work with our community partners, such as the Families for Life movement, to build up an ecosystem that nurtures strong families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: To truly make Singapore a place where all families can thrive, we will need a collective, whole-of-society approach.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: Everyone has a part to play, from individuals and families, to employers and communities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Social and Family Development)
text: Let us all work together to realise our vision of a Singapore Made For Families.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, I have some suggestions which I hope that the Government could consider.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This signals that beyond the actual cost of raising a child, there are more deep-rooted issues that put off Singaporeans from starting a family.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: During my house visits, I have met families with four, five and, sometimes, six children.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They do not live in a big flat and everyone has to share their bedroom.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But they tell me that they are happy that they get to share their joys and the simple pleasures in life with one another.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But I have also met couples with one child, who tell me that it is too expensive to raise a child in Singapore and that they are unable to afford to have a second.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The difference in attitudes reflects a difference towards what each value in life.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I believe that this is shaped, in many ways, by their home environment and, crucially, their work environment.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The work-life balance or, in some cases, the lack of work-life balance, will affect decisions on how working people choose to allocate their time and energy when it comes to work and family roles.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: A 2022 study that examined stress in balancing between work and family among working parents in Hong Kong found that those who have children reported higher levels of work-life stress, possibly due to the additional load of balancing caregiving duties with work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The agencies can study if there is a correlation between quality of work-life balance and the number of staff in the company that choose to start a family.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The outcome of the study can inform agencies with insights into certain work practices that need to be adopted, or perhaps even legislated, to provide Singaporeans with a more conducive work environment to start a family.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: One such work practice would be flexible work arrangements, including work-from-home arrangements, where possible, if the work can be done remotely.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: COVID-19 has shown all of us that flexible work arrangements can work and the Labour Movement strongly believes that this should be an option when the job scope allows for it.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: There should also be clearer norms on after-hours work communications, so that we can give families protected time and for young couples to spend more time together and to start a family.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It has been close to three years since we launched the Tripartite Advisory on Mental Well-being at Workplaces, guiding employers on establishing a work-life harmony policy to offer clarity on after-hours work communication.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Three years on, can the Government consider elevating this advisory into a tripartite standard?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Flexible work arrangements are currently encouraged as part of a tripartite standard.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Some heads of department provide them with the flexibility to come into the office only when absolutely necessary, such as when there are in-person meetings and discussions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They also tell me that their senior management make a conscious effort in informing them that emails sent after office hours need not be replied until the next working day, unless the email is marked as urgent.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: These measures have allowed them to strike a better work-life balance, with more time to focus on the family.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I urge other employers to mimic the Public Service in providing progressive flexible work arrangements and in setting clear after-hours work communication expectations to all their staff.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Lastly, I would like to ask MSF to consider providing adoptive and foster parents with a greater differentiation in benefits under the Act.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Adoptive and foster parents often have to deal with a myriad of problems that are more complicated than a traditional family setting.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We should, therefore, provide them with more support, such as more Government-Paid Paternity Leave and Unpaid Infant Care Leave.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While we acknowledge that the Government has done much in supporting Singaporeans who wish to start a family, we can do more to help shift some of the structural issues that discourage Singaporeans from having children.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We should also provide greater support to adoptive and foster parents.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, we also wring our hands in despair at the stubbornly low total fertility rate or TFR despite over two decades of the Baby Bonus Scheme and its frequent enhancements.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It should thus be more clear than ever that financial considerations are only a part of decisions that parents make about whether or not to start or add to a family.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The amendments proposed by the Bill do go beyond cash payments to address the concerns that we have raised time and again in this House to bring in changes relating to the extinct parental leave system.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: At the heart of parental leave is an acknowledgment of the important role that parents play in their children's lives, particularly in the early days, weeks and months.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How often have we young parents heard people telling us that the days are long but the years are short?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Time spent at work away from our little ones is time that we will never get back.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, for those of us fortunate enough to have kids who go through the milestones of a first smile, a first step, a first word, the first wobbly tooth that falls, know too well the bittersweet thrill that accompanies these moments.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It brings with it a flood of memories and also the realisation that your child is growing up.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, on a personal and also societal level, we are torn by various considerations beyond the urge to want to seize every precious moment with our children.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, we do not exist on fresh air and sunshine.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: So, how do we strike that delicate and constantly shifting balance between ensuring that economic and material needs are fulfilled, alongside ensuring the well-being of our child?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This question gets evermore important in a rapidly disrupted world also facing the twin pressures of cost of living and climate emergency crises that show scant respect for borders.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Added to that, we have heard from many fathers about their desire to play an even greater role in bringing up their children, not only for reasons of personal joy, but also because there are benefits to children's development through more gender equitable socialisation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Some researchers, for example, argue that modelling of gender equitable relationships in child rearing correlates to girls being more ambitious in their working lives.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These social and economic reasons are why the Workers' Party 2020 manifesto called for a total of 24 weeks parental leave to be made mandatory, to be shared between parents of all newborns as they deem fit for their family circumstances, with a minimum of 16 weeks to the mother and four weeks to the father.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Government has also indicated that there are plans to make this change mandatory in due course, and this cannot come soon enough and I hope that we have a firm commitment about when this is expected to happen.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is interesting too, that in Sweden with the highest levels of female labour force participation in the world, parents are entitled to a total of 480 days of paid parental leave, with 90 days reserved for each spouse that cannot be transferred.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Single parents are entitled to all 480 days in recognition of the harder job that they have in bringing up their children.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Latest statistics show that fathers currently take up 30% of all paid parental leave entitlements.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I am not suggesting that we blindly copy the examples in other countries.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We have come far in our journey to support families in the workplace.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We have mandatory parental newborn leave and childcare leave schemes that have been introduced.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I do not doubt that this change is the result of the tireless work of all involved to change mindsets surrounding the support that parents and aspiring parents need from the workplace.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What I believe we can benefit from though, is to closely study the causative effect of flexible and generous parental leave entitlements where parents can exercise more choice in deciding what split works best for their family using the examples of, for example, Sweden described above, with its high female labour force participation rate and gender equity.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But to ensure continued progress, we should also automatically publicly track the uptake of the Government-Paid Paternity Leave (GPPL) taken by fathers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While tracking the uptake of the new four weeks of GPPL taken by fathers, could MSF also survey and study the reasons why fathers do not utilise their full GPPL entitlements?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Anecdotally, we have heard that it is a matter of culture as well.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Pressure from employers alongside wider societal norms are reasons why fathers do not take up paternal leave.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I also note that there is still a gap between an extension of such support to self-employed parents and those without full employment benefits.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Self-employed parents or those not in full-time employment may end up feeling rushed to hurry back to work which in turn may end up with detrimental effects for both parents and children and also make it more stressful for such parents when deciding whether or not to have a child or to add to their family.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Beyond mandating mandatory leave days, we must ultimately look to the trust that we should and can build in the workplace in order to make it more conducive for young parents.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I myself benefited hugely from having had a boss and department where my team understood that sometimes having children makes it difficult for you to be at your desk in the office constantly and that a reasonable amount of give and take should apply.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For us, this could come in the form of having to make an unscheduled school run to pick up a child who started having a fever in the middle of the school day or the flexibility to work from home in the mornings in order to spend more time with an infant who is still breastfeeding.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: All of this was on the understanding that colleagues were ultimately responsible for doing their jobs conscientiously and timeously and that we would support each other in achieving our goals as a team.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is similar to the conversation that we had about our medical certificate (MC) culture, which emerged during the coronavirus pandemic.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This level of trust being common in workplaces may be dismissed as being unrealistic, as being naïve.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While we are acutely aware that there are immediate business continuity costs associated with having to cover the work to be done with employees who are on parental leave, we must continue to look at the bigger picture.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Businesses, ultimately benefit by being able to access a wider hiring pool when they are able to make reasonable accommodations for parents who have care responsibilities and the economy also benefits when we take these measures to support parenthood aspirations and address our low TFR.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While the amendment Bill today focuses on parental leave it would also be remiss of us not to bring up the importance of how it remains to look at the bigger picture.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This means looking beyond traditional population and economic growth models and strategies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As I said in my speech during the Baby Support Grant in 2020, we have to continue to seek sustainable solutions for how to afford the financial and unpaid cost associated with caring for an increasingly aged society while maintaining international and inter-generational fairness.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The number also does not include children who are suffering from other health conditions, both mental and physical, who also warrant extra care from their families and caregivers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Greater awareness of an empathy for families of children with additional needs is undoubtedly growing but do we really understand and account for the larger amount of resources, mental load and emotional costs that parents bear when providing care for such children?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Do we also pay attention and try to address the increased pressure that siblings of children with special needs often bear?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Parents of such children are often faced with both having to strive to give the best support available to their children while at the same time dealing with their own complex emotions, which may involve grief and feelings of loss associated with not being able to achieve dreams of their children doing things that so many of us take for granted sharing.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Cheering their children on at football matches or Sports Days, graduation day, or even just curling up on the sofa with a book, and which can be quickly followed by devastating guilt for feeling such grief in spite of the deep love they continue to hold for their child.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I previously spoke about parental burnout and its lack of systematic quantification.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I believe this is even more important for such families if we are to be serious about property supporting them.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While we call on our policies to do more, I believe that each one of us can start today by showing more empathy and understanding and non-judgement towards our fellow Singaporeans who may be finding it difficult to juggle it all.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And if we are privileged enough to be able to take on a little bit more in any way in the hope that it can ease their burden, just a little, let us do so without complaint or expecting anything in return.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The increase in paternity leave is very much welcomed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is something very close to my heart and this change sends a strong signal about the important role that fathers play.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It also signals that the Government is listening, listening to concerns on the ground and listening to our repeated questions in this House on these important issues, although we sometimes get the same repeated replies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But this Bill also does not include many things that so many of us are still fighting for and I hope that changes will be made as we move towards a more inclusive society and a Singapore Made for Families.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on equalising parental leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a point I have raised repeatedly and will raise again and again, because it is an important point.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Just last year, Minister Josephine Teo spoke about whether equalising parental leave would better reflect the desire for equal sharing of responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She said, “Questions like these should not be forgotten.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Every now and then, we should revisit them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And even if we do not, Mr Louis Ng will make sure that we do.” We should revisit this every now and then.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I raised this earlier this year and will raise it again now.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad we have doubled paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But can go further to eventually equalise parental leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am heartened that Minister Indranee Rajah has said that the Government will continue to work with the tripartite partners to review the scope for more parental leave provisions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I fully understand this is not a one-year, two-year, or even three-year road map.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our four weeks of paternity leave will take time to catch up with the 16 weeks of maternity leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I agree with Minister Indranee Rajah who said that the two parts of the equation are fathers taking up paternity leave and employers being supportive of fathers going on paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our employers will need time to adjust to equalising paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let us help our employers by providing them with the roadmap they need for business certainty.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should also remember that an Institute for Policy Studies (IPS) study highlighted that our policies signal that childcare is a woman’s responsibility and reinforces gender stereotypes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Equalising parental leave is a step forward towards reducing these gender stereotypes and I hope the Government will seriously consider this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I am heartened that as part of the Made for Families initiative, the Government is providing more support for families by increasing unpaid infant care leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the same spirit, I hope we can consider including introducing childcare sick leave for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This, I have raised many times as well and I wish it was part of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is important for the health of our children and for families.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Recently, a teacher emailed me to share her struggles with her child who is constantly falling ill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She told me that her child is always falling sick and had already been hospitalised twice for pneumonia and acute bronchitis.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She told me that the number of childcare leave is really not enough.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She said: "I feel the horrible lack of childcare leave days in Singapore has resulted in parents sending their sick kids to school, which in turn increases the infection rates and causes kids to fall sick easily.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have personally heard colleagues and friends saying that they send their kids to school as long as they don’t have a fever because they just have no choice due to the number of leave days.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As a parent who tries her best to keep her child at home till he recovers, this is very frustrating because my child falls sick again a few days after returning to school." This teacher ended her email by saying that, “Although I am passionate about teaching and impacting the lives of the younger ones, such experiences leave me thinking that I should leave the service, which is a waste.” Her story is not unusual.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is no different from what we are already doing for civil servants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My final point is on a group of parents who are often overlooked and discriminated against – single unwed parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I know this is not part of the Bill today, but it really should be.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This money is not a luxury but a lifeline for so many single unwed parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Since 2016, I have spoken up nine times for extending the Working Mother’s Child Relief, the Parenthood Tax Rebate and the cash component of the Baby Bonus to single unwed parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will be my 10th time raising this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is not about incentivising or disincentivising any behaviours.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Seventeen years ago, Minister Indranee who was a backbencher in this House said, “The third group of people who do not really feel included are the single unwed mothers who are not allowed to rent Housing and Development Board (HDB) flats.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do strongly feel that this is an outdated policy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have spoken on this before, and I understand that the rationale is that the Ministry of National Development (MND) does not want to encourage them to have babies out of wedlock.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But if this is the policy objective, it is not working, because there are many children born out of wedlock.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As I have said before, the availability of rental flats is not something that the couple have in mind when they engage in the activity that results in the child.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That is the last thought on their minds.” I am quite sure that before the couple have sex, they similarly do not think about the cash component of the Baby Bonus.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: President Tharman Shanmugaratnam said in 2013 that single unwed mothers need more help than others, including in the area of financial assistance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He said, “We’re all in this together and the Government will do its part.” It has been 10 years since his speech.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government has, indeed, done more for single unwed parents, but it can do even more.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In our national pledge, we pledge to build a democratic society based on justice and equality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill will make timely and necessary improvements to the Child Development Co-Savings Act as we continue to design and implement a Singapore Made for Families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Since 1987, when Singapore ended its "Stop at Two" population policy, a range of pro-natalist initiatives have been introduced.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: These include paid maternity and paternity leave, childcare subsidies, tax relief, rebates, cash gifts and grants.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Despite these considerable efforts, Singapore is still struggling to encourage couples to marry and, when married, to have children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This decline can be attributed to two key factors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: First, more people are staying single or getting married later in life; and second, married couples are waiting longer to have their first child and having fewer children overall.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Both of these factors are influenced by evolving cultural, social and economic circumstances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Women are increasingly questioning the expectation to marry early, have children and stay at home to look after their children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Women are increasingly able to access independent and financially rewarding careers, both within and outside the marriage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: And women are increasingly aware of the significant cost of raising children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: These initiatives are particularly vital for women who historically bear child-rearing responsibilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Gender equality is crucial for Singapore's continued success, as emphasised in the 2022 White Paper on Singapore Women's Development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: To achieve this, we must maintain women's rights, make family life enriching and continuously engage Singaporean girls and women’s perspectives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: On that note, I would like to highlight a study, “The Aspirations of Singapore Muslim Women”, carried out by the non-profit organisation, Singapore Muslim Women’s Association (PPIS), in 2021.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The study revealed that Muslim women’s top family aspirations include work-life balance, financial stability and the ability to raise children well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is heartening to note that over the years, our Government has implemented policies to encourage married persons in Singapore to have more children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As mentioned, I welcome the changes in the Bill as it aims to provide additional support to make child-rearing an appealing and affordable option for couples.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, I seek some clarifications about some of the proposed amendments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Before I do so, I would like to share my personal experience as a mother who benefited from the Child Development Co-Savings Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In 2001, I was working full-time as a Probation Officer with the Ministry of Community Development and Sports.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In May of that year, my second child was born and he qualified for the Baby Bonus Scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This greatly eased the financial strain of raising two young children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: My first-born, who was two-and-a-half years old at that time, was eagerly waiting for his "Thambi", or “brother” in Tamil, and could not understand why his baby brother spent most of his time sleeping.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In his excitement to play with his brother, he threw a toy police car into his crib.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Interestingly, both my boys later completed their National Service with the Singapore Police Force (SPF) and I believe the toy police car may have played a part in that.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As a working mother, it was difficult to supervise and care for two children under the age of three and keeping them both safe was my utmost priority.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: My eldest child attended childcare, a direct benefit of the Baby Bonus Scheme, and my mother took care of the baby.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I was also very fortunate to have supervisors who believed in measuring performance by outcomes and who allowed me to work from home.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This was an immense relief and I would not have been able to balance my responsibilities as a mother and a Probation Officer without the support of my supervisors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I consider myself privileged to have received emotional support from my mother; financial support from the Government by way of the Baby Bonus; and practical support from my employer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: These opportunities allowed me to work from home, excel in my career and continue my education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Importantly, these opportunities allowed me to be a mother to my two wonderful children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: These amendments will assist to ensure the quality and professionalism of health and educational services provided by approved persons to children and their families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: What support is given to approved persons when suspended to help them regain their approval?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: If an approved person can no longer serve a child or a family due to suspension or revocation, what are their obligations in arranging alternative care, especially if they provide childcare services?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Will the proposed duties for officers and employees of approved persons include an understanding of policies and procedures necessary to safeguard children who access their services?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: How are we promoting more equal parenting roles in households, especially during paternity leave, considering gender imbalances?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I appreciate Members’ attention and I would like to conclude by sharing remarks from Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat during the launch of "A Singapore Made for Families 2025" in November 2022.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: On that occasion, he noted, and I quote: "Establishing a supportive and adaptable work environment for employees to achieve work-life harmony is not only pro-family but also pro-business.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Workers who can balance their work and family responsibilities are better able to contribute effectively at their workplaces." Clarifications notwithstanding, I conclude in support of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: More recently, amendments were introduced to avail benefits to birth, adoptive and stillborn parents in different employment situations.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Ten years is a good time to take stock and see how the policy can be improved upon.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The experience of other developed countries suggests that prioritising paternity leave has a positive impact on parents, caregivers, their employers and, most importantly, the children.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: One of the most notable examples of this is Iceland, where parents now get 12 months of leave, six months for each parent, with six weeks of that being transferable.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: That shift that started in the year 2000, when paternity leave was increased from two weeks to three months was rapid and, today, more than 90% of fathers take paternity leave.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is normal and socially expected to see men out pushing their babies in a pram, and the research shows that men are experiencing the role as a father much more strongly and in a more positive way, for instance, being around for their babies’ first steps or first words.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: World Health Organization (WHO) research shows that Icelandic daddies enjoy the stronger position as fathers in the world, with children finding it easy to go to daddy whenever they have a problem.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The statistics also show that it has reduced the gender pay gap, as mothers are able to return to work and normal working hours sooner, because childcare is more equally divided between both parents.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We are some way away from this in Singapore, where women still take on much more childcare responsibilities, even when working full-time.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But if we want greater equality of opportunity for women, we need to provide greater equality for men at home.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Is it a missed opportunity to signal the will to take firm steps, by making this shift voluntary rather than mandatory?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Is it a missed opportunity to signal an intent to work towards narrowing or closing the gap between maternity and paternity leave, even if a practical approach is taken in implementation?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Many multinational companies already provide significantly longer paternity leave than the current two-week requirement, some equal to maternity leave and with no tenure requirement.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These companies see a generational shift in their workforce.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Paternity leave is part of their strategy to attract, engage and retain talent.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In doing so, they have also had to be more intentional in rolling out supporting measures like flexible work arrangements, in line with the direction of travel that we have already set out on.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: More companies should be made to see this as a first step, by making it mandatory or at least committing to a timeline in the not-too-distant future, rather than the current wait-and-see stance and by kickstarting a conversation about the importance of parental leave equality in promoting shared care.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: At this point, I would like to ask a clarification of the Minister.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Moving to the increase in unpaid infant care leave from six days to 12 days, on paper, sounds good.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But what is the current take-up rate of unpaid infant care leave today?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And the anecdotes suggest that above and beyond the subtle pressures that discourage fathers from using paternity leave, many fathers experience sometimes not so subtle pressures when it comes to taking unpaid infant care leave, even if they are willing to forgo the pay.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I would also like to ask a clarification to the Minister if the use of unpaid infant care leave will be tracked going forward.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For many, six days is simply not enough.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These are the real-life stories of my Woodlands residents.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Like Mr E, who has 4 children aged one, three, five and eight, who works 12-hour shifts at a manufacturing plant.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: His wife works 9.00 am to 5.00 pm.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, they are lucky to have their children in infant care and childcare at PCF Sparkletots so she can drop them off and pick them up after work.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But every once in a while, one of the children will come back from school sick and when one child gets sick, it is an inevitability that it gets passed to one or more of the other children.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And suddenly, they are faced with having to keep the kids at home for three, four, five days, a week.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This happens three to four times a year.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And we know that one bout of HFMD means seven days of MC for the child.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Since six days of their childcare leave are already used on the six days that the centre closes, they end up using a fair chunk of their annual leave when their children are sick.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Mr K is a private hire driver with four children aged nine, 12, 13 and 15.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: His wife is a homemaker, caring for the children and for her mother who is a stroke patient.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Each morning, he drives his children to four different schools, before starting to accept jobs, even though this means he misses out on some of more lucrative driving slots.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Sometimes, he gets calls from the school to pick up his daughter when she is sick or from his wife to bring her mother to her medical appointment or his daughter to her developmental assessments, which further reduces his driving hours.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He sometimes thinks about going back to the IT sector which will likely give him better career development prospects.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But he feels he needs the flexibility that being a private hire driver gives him given his family circumstances.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And Mdm S, a single mother with two children aged eight and 17, who works in the healthcare sector.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Each weekday morning, Mdm S sees her daughters off to school and then goes to work, secure with the knowledge that her mother will be there to watch her daughter when she is back from school at around 2.00 pm.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But her mother recently suffered a stroke and is now in a nursing home.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, now, when her younger daughter gets out of school, she relies on a combination of friends, neighbours and her siblings' care to watch over her until her shift ends at 9.00 pm.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And given that a 17-year-old often has other plans, that often means leaving the eight-year-old child alone for several hours a day.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As a single mother, there are only two days of childcare leave available for her when her daughter falls ill.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Their stories demonstrate the increasing varied situations and complex challenges working parents face and the trade-offs that they make on a daily basis to care for their children, including when they get sick.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Each of them must weave together a different patchwork of solutions often based on family-specific factors, such as income, the number and ages of their children, along with the availability of grandparents, relatives, neighbours and domestic helpers and on the nature of their work and workplace dynamics.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Government has stated that one of its key priorities is to ensure that parents have access to quality and affordable childcare and for their parents, and is increasing the number of childcare spaces.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But the cost of childcare is still cited as a reason for couples to delay or forgo children.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And what happens when the child falls sick?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For many parents, there is no alternative or safe place to take their child when he or she needs to be taken out of childcare for the day.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Grandparents may be too old or live a distance far away or deceased, while leaving the care of a sick child to a helper may not be a solution they feel comfortable with.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And indeed, some young parents find the mere suggestion of these solutions to be quite triggering.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Fortunately, there are an increasing number of progressive companies that have implemented family-friendly practices – childcare leave, flexible work arrangements and more broadly, a supportive workplace culture.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Yet, the Government has been slow to move to legislate further enhancements to childcare leave, citing a need to strike a balance in addressing the caregiving needs of parents and the manpower and operational needs of employers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This is especially so for small and medium enterprises (SMEs), some of which may still be grappling with the effects of the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is concern that mandating more childcare leave might affect employability.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is not uncommon to hear managers and co-workers, especially singles or adults with no children, expressing annoyance or frustration with having to cover for colleagues who go on childcare leave at short notice.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Singles or adults with no children often complain that they often end up caring for their elderly parent while their siblings with children excuse themselves, with even less support for parental care leave and financial support.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And on the flipside, some parents with sick children who have to take more days, speak of feeling resigned to what they see as retribution in their performance appraisals and bonuses, particularly if they have ambitious single bosses or older bosses who have forgotten what it like to have a young family.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Fundamentally, we must all have more empathy for others, more respect for all.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This cannot simply be a campaign slogan for one, but a movement for all and we must work, Government and citizens, to make it happen.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But there are things we can do in the nearer team.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Government has committed significant funding to making a Singapore Made for Families, from higher Baby Bonuses, contributions to Child Development Account (CDA) and the proposed increase in paternity and unpaid infant leave.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, a slew of initiatives are underway to support women's development, especially towards women at the workforce and in the community.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is also growing focus on our ageing population, on single moms, on special needs children.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Meanwhile, even with the sceptre of a recession, some sectors are still struggling to get enough manpower, including high demand sectors like healthcare and education, which also hire more women.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The stars therefore seem to be aligned for stakeholders to act on the importance of sufficient childcare leave.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Given these, I urge the Government to consider two further enhancements today.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There seems to be enough parents across a range of family and work circumstances for whom an additional two days per child would make a material difference and enough evidence that improved benefits drive employee engagement and business results.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Second, taking an industry specific lens to enhancing childcare and childcare leave and driving customised solutions for each industry in partnership with employers and unions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Working parents faces different constraints and preferences for key aspects of childcare, such as type of care, location and hours.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This calls for a more de-averaged approach that pays attention to the difference in caregiver experiences, looks for gaps in care-specific to each industry and develops customised solutions that better meet those employees' needs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Just as we have industry transformation maps that drive skills, that drive productivity solutions and workforce development at the sector level, the transformation to more family-friendly environments can be driven at the sector level.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our approach must be to give all families, parents and children, more help, whatever their choices and ambitions and around increasingly varied needs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We have made progressive enhancements to providing this support and choice, while maintaining our pro-business stance.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But we need to go further and faster.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I am confident we can continue to find innovative solutions to this.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I count myself lucky to be a Singaporean.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore ranks as one of the best countries to live in for a woman.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: We advocate equal rights for women and men, at work and at home.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I thank the Minister for the Child Development Co-Savings (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: We can do more to advance gender equality and empathy for working caregivers at three levels – Government, organisation and the individual.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, this troubles the self-employed private hire car driver or hawker.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Regardless of the circumstance, the self-employed private hire car driver or hawker must pay rent for his car or hawker stall, seven days a week and rent is a significant expense.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Likely, he must dip into his savings to cover rent, other expenses and lost income.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This is a tall order for many self-employed persons.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: A self-employed driver or hawker thus hopes that the Government can enhance the calculation of paid paternity leave, from 24 days to 28 days.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Doing so would allow the self-employed person to wholeheartedly embrace his duties as a supportive spouse and a father to a newborn.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, could the Minister consider providing paid paternity leave to the self-employed father for the full four-week period of lost income?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Employees' expectations of work and work-life balance have changed.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: They take on multiple responsibilities at work and juggle various caregiving roles at home.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Employees thus seek balance and fulfilment, even as organisations pursue rejuvenation and growth.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: They must also evolve structures, policies and processes to meet changing aspirations.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Imagine these possibilities: structures that make work schedules and back-ups predictable?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: They give employees the leeway to balance dynamic family and work needs.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: They allow employees to prioritise tasks and manage deadlines.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Work processes that accommodate both organisation and employees' needs?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: They empower managers to be empathetic and employees, especially frontliners, to be comfortable about making time for themselves and their families.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Like getting organisations onboard digital solutions, we can transform these possibilities into reality.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: We can expect forward-looking organisations to turn to the Government for guidance and resources to create family-supportive workplaces.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: These organisations are keen because they know that their employees want to be empowered as professionals and supported as breadwinners and caregivers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Government consider helping these organisations to create work environments supportive of caregivers in their workforce?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This means that 3.8 working-age people of ages 20 to 64 were providing economic support to a dependant aged 65 years or older.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Compare this with 10 years ago, when nearly two times more working age people were supporting a mature dependant.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: As society ages and family units shrink, every working person matters more so than ever.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Many of us might know of women in our networks who had to give up their careers to become full-time caregivers because they felt that support was lacking.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, could the Government consider expanding caregiving support to cater for more types of caregiving needs?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, caregiving-related leave would benefit workers, especially those in frontline roles.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I recall negotiating for urgent leave on behalf of a union member.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: She was a retail assistant who had to leave work halfway because an older family member suddenly took ill.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: It was a trying ordeal for her and me.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: She was also very stressed because she had to offset the urgent leave against her meagre earned leave balance.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Caregiving leave would have been a more direct and immediate way for her and other frontline workers to respond to urgent family needs.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Organisations that establish flexible work and family-supportive policies would welcome more recognition and support as these encourage their employees who are caregivers to stay on.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: A monologue from the recent movie, "Barbie", took the world by storm because it shone a light on the unrealistic expectations that women are held to.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I quote a memorable line that proclaims that women "have to be a career woman, but also always be looking out for other people." How true that is!

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: It could be enhanced by providing a differentiated approach for self-employed individuals.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For self-employed parents, they hope to be granted Government-Paid Paternity or Maternity Leave that is calculated using a weekly index of seven days.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: They also hope that the Government could consider disbursing the claim amount at the start of the paternity or maternity leave period than after the leave period has concluded.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Disbursing at the outset of the leave period would help to alleviate the financial strain that the self-employed person has during this period of lost income.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Organisations play a role in supporting employees' use of the enhanced leaves set out in this Bill and the Child Development Co-savings Act.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Organisations could benefit from more recognition and support to develop and sustain family-supportive workplaces.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: With this, Mr Speaker, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: At its heart, this Bill calls for an embrace of a collaborative journey that encompasses fathers and mothers alike in the nurturing of our future generations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I would like to seek several clarifications on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, I have clarifications about the adoption and effectiveness of the policies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To ensure success, we must address the matter of take-up and track its efficacy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While it is heartening to witness fathers exercising their leave entitlement, there remains concerns and apprehension about negative performance evaluations due to extended leave-taking.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This worry is likely to persist even when employees are wholly entitled to their leave privileges.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we ensure that fathers who fully utilise their paternity leave will not face hindered career advancements or negative performance evaluations?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the Ministry work with companies to explore practical avenues to encourage more fathers to utilise their entitled leave allocation?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Undoubtedly, there are numerous advantages to greater paternal involvement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The proposed amendments currently provide that the Government will reimburse employers who voluntarily allow extra paternity leave for a period not exceeding two weeks.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could we not take a more assertive stance?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could we consider making this extended paternity leave mandatory rather than voluntary?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Speaker, Sir, we should examine the financial implications and mechanisms of administering these provisions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: An important parallel concern pertains to the authenticity of claims for such leave and benefits.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Drawing lessons from past experiences such as the over disbursement during the COVID-19 Jobs Support Scheme, we need robust measures in place.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Does the Bill empower the Ministry to retrieve funds that have been erroneously disbursed?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, is there a dedicated unit within MSF that handles such disputes?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What measures are in place to recover funds from employers who may have inadvertently allowed the error to take place?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I ask this because lower-wage employees may have spent the money and may not be able to make repayment as quickly.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Also, putting some responsibility on the employer may resolve some of the administrative issues that the Government may face as regards to the disbursements of these funds.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A broader perspective necessitates us to examine the impact on the workforce left behind who shoulder the responsibilities of those on paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we ensure that the workplace remains efficient and productive during these absences, safeguarding against undue strain on those who continue to serve?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must acknowledge the valid concerns raised by singles who often find themselves shouldering additional responsibilities due to their marital status, which can lead to feelings of inequity and being discriminated against.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Thus, we must delve into the effects these changes might have on businesses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we strike a balance that supports families while recognising the operational challenges businesses might face?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we support companies like SMEs who have lesser employees and may feel more constraints when employees go on paternity leave?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, it is worth considering the consolidation of various existing leave schemes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: At present, an array of leave options is available, classified under marriage and family leave by the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP).

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These include childcare, eldercare, maternity, paternity and a more encompassing family care leave.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: TAFEP merely recommends potential leave schemes for companies to adopt.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Given the current landscape, can we explore amalgamating these leave schemes and rendering them fungible?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For example, we could introduce a family care leave scheme to heighten flexibility for both parents and caregivers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The move toward amalgamation aligns with the evolving needs of our society as more people are choosing to prioritise their loved ones over work if they may afford to do so.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Drawing from my experience as a father of five, I have witnessed the pivotal role of paternal involvement in shaping our children's lives.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Research reinforces this notion, indicating that the impact starts prior to birth.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Partner support during pregnancy links to improved maternal health and better outcomes for mothers and infants.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Extensive studies consistently highlight the positive effects of active father involvement on children, spanning from enhanced self-esteem and reduced behavioural problems to heightened social competence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Remarkably, these benefits often shape the trajectory of the next generation, with children raised by engaged fathers becoming involved parents themselves.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But embracing the role of an active and engaged father presents an array of challenges.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Utilising my designated paternity leave to care for my newborn was but a fleeting moment within the grander journey.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If you ask my wife, she will say that those two weeks flew by so fast, they were almost negligible!

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This stems from the fact that child-rearing is an uninterrupted, daily commitment we undertake as parents – a commitment that extends until our children reach a stage of independence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Transformative change cannot be achieved through a single or few policies within a short timeframe.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, we cannot simply replicate solutions from other countries due to our unique context.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But we must concede the indisputable significance of work-life balance and the cultural ethos in nurturing a society that offers Singaporeans the confidence and assurance to embrace parenthood.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Encouraging fathers to embrace an active role in nurturing their children goes beyond the allocation of paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Beyond this defined leave period, fathers must continue to strategise their time during work weeks to cultivate meaningful family connections.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It necessitates purposeful allocation and investment of time.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In times of family emergencies, the understanding and accommodation of employers and colleagues become paramount.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):  	Therefore, we need a collective whole-of-society effort.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I look forward to hearing your maiden speech in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: At that time, Singapore was alarmed with a declining birth rate.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The popularly known Baby Bonus Scheme was born.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Its message was clear and unmistakable – to encourage family building and to renew our population.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Fast forward to the present, family dynamics have shifted and the Government's response?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I wholeheartedly welcome this decision and I support the change.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It again sends a resounding message – parental responsibility is a joint effort and not just a mother's duty.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This House is no stranger to the undeniable benefits of active fathers and I commend the Government for championing this.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It is clear when the Government recognises the changing needs of our society, the Government responds and acts.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This group I am referring to are parents of children with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: They too deserve the attention and response from the Government.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This means that about 30 newborns out of a thousand live births are born with disabilities every year.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Children with disabilities often require more specialised care and incur higher expenses than their peers.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Their parents shoulder additional financial, physical and emotional challenges.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: These are challenges they do not see coming; challenges that affect all income levels.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
